design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects (DerSimonian and Laird) meta-analysis of the dose-response association between level of cannabis use and psychosis-related outcomes. Within each study, people were ranked on that study's own ordinal cannabis measure and given an index from 0 (never used) to 1 (the most-exposed rank), people who had used being spread uniformly over bins sized by the group counts; individual-level data were then simulated from the published case and non-case counts at each level (the authors' earlier method, Vassos et al., 2012) and a logistic regression of outcome on the index was fitted. The pooled slope gives the odds ratio between the most-exposed rank and never use. Only crude counts were pooled. Search to 31 December 2013; 18 studies in the systematic review, 10 in the meta-analysis (6 prospective cohorts, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 case-control study), 66,816 individuals.
can_establish: Whether, in ten observational studies published up to 2013, people ranked higher on each study's own ordinal measure of cannabis use had higher crude odds of a psychosis-related outcome than people who never used cannabis, and the size and spread of that crude gradient on a common rank scale.
cannot_establish: Causation or its direction (no pooled estimate is adjusted for any confounder, and four of the ten studies are cross-sectional or case-control); the risk at any absolute frequency, amount, duration or potency of use, because the top of the rank scale is a different exposure in each study (more than 50 lifetime occasions among Swedish conscripts, daily use in the London case-control sample, regular use in nine Finnish adolescents); adjusted absolute risks (crude proportions by level can be computed from Table 1, for example admission with schizophrenia in 215 of 36,429 Swedish conscripts who had never used cannabis and 28 of 731 who had used it more than 50 times, about 6 and 38 in 1,000, editors' calculation, with follow-up not stated); or whether the gradient is linear, which the model assumes rather than tests.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO from inception to 31 December 2013, combining dose-related terms (dose-response, daily use, duration, high frequency, heavy use) with psychosis or schizophrenia terms and cannabis or marijuana terms; reference lists of the included studies and of five earlier reviews were checked and experts were contacted (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The pooled primary studies are prospective cohorts from the USA, New Zealand, Sweden (1969 conscripts), Germany and England (two), cross-sectional surveys from Australia (two) and Finland (adolescents), and the London first-episode case-control sample of the Genetics and Psychosis (GAP) study (Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed cohort and cross-sectional studies that measured cannabis use with a dose criterion (frequency, amount or severity) before the onset of psychosis, classified it into at least three levels (never use plus two or more), and established psychosis-related outcomes with validated clinical measures; no language limit. Excluded: samples with mental illness before cannabis use or at ultra-high risk; studies of comorbidity between substance use disorders and psychosis; neuropsychological or schizoid-trait outcomes; studies of age at onset only (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph). For the meta-analysis, studies with continuous outcomes were left out, one of three reports on the Swedish conscripts was kept, one study with 10 cases was dropped, and the two published GAP reports were replaced by updated data supplied by the authors (Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Not reported at review level. Table 1 gives only country, design, exposure measure, outcome and counts; no ages, sex or recruitment settings are given. The share of each pooled sample that had used cannabis ranges from 5.6% (Finnish adolescents) to 56.8% (London case-control sample) (editors' arithmetic from Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: The electronic search required dose-related terms, and three of the four studies added by hand were reports of the Swedish conscript cohort (refs 15, 20, 29), which suggests the search was not sensitive (Results, 1st paragraph). Only peer-reviewed articles were sought, with no grey literature, and the search closed on 31 December 2013, about 25 months before online publication on 15 February 2016. Eight of the 18 systematic-review studies were not pooled and two of them are not identified. The London case-control data are the review team's own: the second author is first author of both published GAP reports (refs 16 and 31), and the pooled data were updated data on the same sample provided by the authors (Figure 1).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used, always as an ordered variable (Table 1): lifetime frequency (US cohort, Swedish conscripts, Finnish adolescents, English cohort of Zammit 2011), frequency at baseline (Australian survey, German cohort), frequency in the past year with dependence as the top level (British survey of Wiles 2006), duration of use in years (Australian young adults of McGrath 2010), use more than three times a year at ages 18 and 15 (New Zealand) and frequency (London case-control study). The rank index gives never use 0 and spreads people who had used over bins of a uniform 0-1 scale sized by the group counts (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: The top category differs by study (Table 1): daily use (USA), weekly use (Australian survey), use more than three times a year by age 15 (New Zealand), more than 50 lifetime occasions (Sweden), almost daily use (Germany), cannabis dependence (British survey), regular use (Finland; 9 people), six or more years of use (Australian young adults), more than 60 occasions (English cohort) and everyday use (London). Potency and period of use were not considered (Discussion, 6th paragraph), and age at first use was not modelled as such, except that in the New Zealand cohort the ordered levels are themselves defined by age (use by 18, use by 15; Table 1); route was not considered.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled. Crude counts were pooled, so tobacco, alcohol and other drug use are not adjusted for in any pooled estimate (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. The authors state that they had no data on the time between regular cannabis use and illness onset (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

comparison.controls: The Methods state that people who had never used cannabis were the reference category (index 0) in every study (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph), but Table 1's reference rows read no cannabis within the last year (Wiles et al., British survey), no cannabis use at age 18 (Arseneault et al., New Zealand) and none or no use for frequency at baseline (Henquet et al., German cohort; Degenhardt and Hall, Australian survey); the reference is no use, as each study measured it.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. No adjustment of any kind: crude odds ratios were recomputed from the case and non-case counts at each exposure level even where a study had reported only adjusted odds ratios (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Nothing premorbid enters the pooled estimates: family history of psychosis, childhood adversity, symptoms or functioning before first use, IQ, ethnicity, socioeconomic position and urbanicity are all unadjusted. The authors name ethnicity and socioeconomic status as possible confounders (Discussion, 6th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported; people who never used cannabis may have used other drugs, and no pooled estimate separates cannabis from other substance use.

outcomes.instruments: Heterogeneous (Table 1): at least one psychotic symptom within one year of follow-up (DSM-III; USA); positive psychosis screener within one year (DSM-IV; Australian survey); schizophreniform disorder at age 26 (DSM-IV; New Zealand); inpatient admission for schizophrenia (ICD-8 and ICD-9; Swedish conscripts); two or more psychotic symptoms on the CIDI psychosis section (Germany); self-reported psychotic symptoms on the Psychosis Screening Questionnaire (British survey); prodromal symptoms on the PROD-screen (Finnish adolescents, where 1937 of 6298 were counted as cases); any CIDI hallucination (Australian young adults); self-reported severe psychotic experiences on the PLIKS questionnaire (English cohort); first-episode psychosis (ICD-10; London). Where a study reported several outcomes, the most severe was used (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the primary studies was done.
outcomes.operationalization: A psychosis-related outcome was either symptoms above each study's threshold or a diagnosis or admission. In the outcome subgroup analysis, eight studies are classed as psychotic symptoms and only two (Swedish admissions for schizophrenia; London first-episode psychosis) as diagnoses (Figure 3B).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five pooled estimates (overall; cohort; cross-sectional; psychotic symptoms; diagnosis), one meta-regression on study year and two small-study tests. The odds ratios for the median person who used cannabis and for the top 20% are transformations of the same pooled slope, not further tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Selection: one author identified studies and a second independently checked them for inclusion; extraction: two authors independently (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled log-odds slope b = 1.36 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.68), I² = 82%, giving an odds ratio of 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34) between the most-exposed rank (index 1) and never use; model-based odds ratios of 1.97 (1.68 to 2.31) for the median person who used cannabis and 3.40 (2.55 to 4.54) for the median of the top 20% (Results, 3rd paragraph). Study estimates at index 1 (Figure 3): Tien 1990, 1.85 (1.33 to 2.57); Zammit 2002, 6.20 (4.19 to 9.17); Henquet 2005, 5.16 (3.13 to 8.50); Wiles 2006, 3.04 (1.41 to 6.59); Zammit 2011, 4.36 (2.38 to 7.99); Arseneault 2002, 4.29 (1.45 to 12.70); Degenhardt 2001, 7.45 (3.99 to 13.90); Miettunen 2008, 4.67 (3.66 to 5.96); McGrath 2010, 1.89 (1.32 to 2.69); GAP data 2012, 4.38 (3.30 to 5.81). Subgroups: cohort 3.83 (2.34 to 6.29); cross-sectional 3.99 (2.50 to 6.37); psychotic symptoms 3.59 (2.42 to 5.32); diagnosis 5.07 (3.62 to 7.09). Meta-regression on year p = .53; Egger p = .79; Begg p = .86 (Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs). Editors' calculation from the ten printed study estimates (DerSimonian and Laird; it reproduces the pooled 3.90 and I² of 82%): Q = 49.3 on 9 degrees of freedom, tau² = 0.19, 95% prediction interval for a new study's odds ratio at index 1 about 1.3 to 11.5; within-subgroup I² about 80% (cohort), 87% (cross-sectional), 82% (symptoms) and 50% (diagnosis, 2 studies).
analysis.covariates: None. Every pooled estimate is crude; adjusted estimates reported by primary studies were not used (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the paper states that the search followed the PRISMA statement (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Cochran's Q, tau², study weights, prediction intervals and subgroup heterogeneity are not reported, although the Methods say Q was used. The 18 systematic-review studies are not listed; two studies left out of the meta-analysis are not named, and the eight unpooled studies are not described beyond their exclusion reasons. The supplement (a Word file, not read) is described only as illustrating the simulation method with an example; no pooled result depends on it.
analysis.power: Not addressed. With ten studies, Egger's and Begg's tests have little power to detect small-study effects, which the paper does not mention; the diagnosis subgroup rests on two studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In ten observational studies (six cohorts, three cross-sectional surveys, one case-control study), crude odds of a psychosis-related outcome rose with rank on each study's own ordinal cannabis measure; the fitted odds ratio between the top rank and never use was 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34), with high heterogeneity (I² 82%; editors' 95% prediction interval about 1.3 to 11.5). The top of the rank scale is a different exposure in each study, and the category-level crude odds ratios in Table 1 do not rise steadily in several studies (for example 0.40 to 0.70 for the three lowest use categories in the London data). Nothing is adjusted for confounding.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that “high levels of cannabis use increase the risk of psychotic outcomes” and that the evidence confirms a dose-response relationship, and the conclusion calls the result “the most accurate estimate of the effect size” (Abstract; Discussion, 9th paragraph). Gaps: (1) a causal verb from crude observational data, in an abstract that also says a causal link cannot be established and does not say the estimates are unadjusted; (2) dose here is a within-study rank, not an amount, frequency or potency, so the gradient cannot be translated into any level of use, and linearity is assumed by the model (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); the consistent increase in every included study (Results, 3rd paragraph) describes the fitted lines of Figure 2, which rise by construction whenever the slope is positive, not the category-level data; (3) reverse causation is called unlikely because cohorts with symptomatic participants at baseline were excluded (Discussion, 1st paragraph), but four of the ten studies are cross-sectional or case-control; (4) the headline 3.90 is the odds ratio for the single most-exposed rank, and the authors themselves say that applying Moore et al.'s average 45% attenuation for adjustment to their top-20% estimate gives results comparable to Moore's 2.1 (Discussion, 7th paragraph), which the abstract does not mention; (5) the stronger association with hard outcomes (5.07) rests on two studies, one of them the authors' own data; (6) the conclusion's public-policy remarks about dose reduction and later onset are not tested by these data.

timeline.event: Earlier reviews by Henquet, Murray, Linszen and van Os (Schizophrenia Bulletin) and by Semple, McIntosh and Lawrie (Journal of Psychopharmacology), cited for an approximately two-fold risk of psychotic disorder in people who use cannabis (Introduction, 1st paragraph).

Moore et al. systematic review, whose pooled odds ratios this review gives as 1.4 for any use and 2.1 for the most frequent use; the authors argue their higher estimate reflects crude data, newer studies and the top-rank extrapolation (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

Di Forti et al., an earlier report on high-potency cannabis from the London GAP case-control study (British Journal of Psychiatry); with the 2014 GAP report (Schizophrenia Bulletin), replaced in this meta-analysis by updated data on the same sample supplied by the authors.

Vassos et al., simulation method for meta-analysing an exposure gradient from grouped counts, first applied to urbanicity and schizophrenia; reused here (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).

Gage, Zammit and Hickman (F1000 Medicine Reports), a review titled as arguing that stronger evidence is needed before accepting an important role for cannabis in the aetiology of schizophrenia; used here only as a source of references, its arguments are not discussed.

Davis et al., US national survey (NESARC): adjusted odds ratio 3.69 (2.49 to 5.47) for a psychosis diagnosis with lifetime cannabis dependence, cited as remarkably similar to this review's estimate (Discussion, 7th paragraph; second-hand figure).

Di Forti et al. (Lancet Psychiatry), GAP case-control analysis of 410 cases and 370 controls from the same London study whose updated data are pooled here; not cited by this review (card sc_di_forti_2015). The two sources overlap and are not independent.
This review: random-effects meta-analysis of a crude rank-scale gradient in ten studies.

Di Forti et al. (EU-GEI, Lancet Psychiatry) cite this meta-analysis as showing a dose-response association with the highest odds in the heaviest use (Introduction, 1st paragraph; card sc_di_forti_2019).

replication.where_it_stands: Often cited as the dose-response meta-analysis for cannabis and psychosis. Its pooled figure is a crude odds ratio extrapolated to the top rank of ten different exposure scales and should only be cited with that description; it cannot give the risk at a stated frequency or potency. The review discusses no critique of a causal reading and no genetic (Mendelian randomization, polygenic score, co-relative) or quasi-experimental test. The London case-control data inside it overlap Di Forti et al. (2009, 2014 and 2015), and five of its six cohorts are the reports Moore et al. (2007) pooled (Tien and Anthony 1990, ECA; Arseneault et al. 2002, Dunedin; Zammit et al. 2002, Swedish conscripts; Henquet et al. 2005, EDSP; Wiles et al. 2006, NPMS; editors' cross-check of the two reference lists), so the two reviews are not independent replications.

funding.funder: Guy's and St Thomas Charity Grant (R080529); the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centre for Mental Health at South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust and Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London; the European Community's Seventh Framework Programme under the Marie Curie Industry-Academia Partnership and Pathways, grant agreement 286213 (Funding section).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest in relation to the subject of the study (Acknowledgment section).
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors are at King's College London, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (Department of Psychosis Studies; MRC SGDP Centre). The second author is first author of both published GAP reports pooled here, and Marconi, Di Forti and Murray are also authors of the GAP case-control paper read for sc_di_forti_2015; Vassos, Murray and Lewis are authors of the simulation method used (ref 24). No procedure for appraising the authors' own study is described. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant meta-analysis of prospective cohorts that recorded frequency, amount and potency of cannabis use before any psychotic symptoms, harmonized onto an absolute scale (for example days of use per month and THC content), adjusted for family history, childhood adversity, other drug use and socioeconomic position, reporting absolute incidence by exposure level and testing rather than assuming a linear gradient.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (any), exposure (level of cannabis use measured with a dose criterion before psychosis, at least three levels), comparator (never use) and outcome (validated psychosis-related measures) are stated (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph).
No protocol or registration is mentioned; the paper says only that the search followed PRISMA.
Cohort and cross-sectional designs were made eligible without explanation, and a case-control study was pooled although the criteria name only cohort and cross-sectional studies.

Three databases, the search terms, reference lists of included studies and five reviews, contact with experts, and no language limit. But the restriction to peer-reviewed articles is not justified, there was no grey-literature or registry search, and the search closed on 31 December 2013, about 25 months before online publication; the dose-term search missed three reports of the Swedish conscript cohort that were found only by hand. Under a reading of AMSTAR 2 that asks for justification of language restrictions only, the item would be partial yes (the project's reading of item 4 is decision p-amstar2-item4).

One author identified studies and a second independently checked them for inclusion (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph); the paper does not say that the second author screened the 571 records or the full texts, so exclusions by the first author were not duplicated. A close call.
Two authors extracted the data independently (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 3rd paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives exclusion reasons by category (for example 53 for unsuitable outcome) and the text names five excluded reports (refs 17, 20, 29, 30, 36), but there is no list of excluded full texts with reasons, and two studies left out of the meta-analysis are not identified. The supplement, not read, is described only as illustrating the simulation method.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, design, exposure measure, outcome with diagnostic system, exposure levels and case and non-case counts for the ten pooled studies; it gives no ages, sex, recruitment setting or follow-up length beyond what the outcome column implies, and the eight systematic-review studies that were not pooled are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the primary studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Crude odds ratios were recomputed from counts and pooled even where studies had reported adjusted estimates (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph); for non-randomized studies AMSTAR 2 asks for adequately adjusted estimates, or a justification for raw data when adjusted ones are unavailable. The rank-index method also assumes the same distribution of cannabis use across studies (5th paragraph), which the exposure categories in Table 1 contradict, and the case-control study is pooled with cohorts and surveys. Random-effects pooling itself is appropriate for I² of 82%.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment, so no analysis of its impact; subgroups by design and outcome type are not a test of study quality.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Bias in individual studies was never assessed. The discussion names confounding by ethnicity and socioeconomic status as a possible partial explanation and then sets it aside by citing two adjusted studies, and argues against reverse causation from an exclusion criterion that does not apply to the four cross-sectional and case-control studies; the abstract states that high levels of use increase the risk.

I² is reported (82%), subgroup analyses by design and outcome and a meta-regression on study year were run, and the discussion addresses the expected heterogeneity (Results, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph). Within-subgroup heterogeneity is not reported; the editors' recomputation from Figure 3 gives I² of 80% to 87% within the larger subgroups, so the subgroups explain little of it.

Egger's (p = .79) and Begg's (p = .86) tests were run and reported (Results, 5th paragraph). Their low power with ten studies is not mentioned and the discussion of possible publication bias is a single sentence; a close call.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a no-conflict statement are given; the paper does not flag that the London case-control data are the authors' own, updated and unpublished.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Six of the seven critical items of AMSTAR 2 are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11 and 13); only item 15 is met, so confidence in the pooled numbers as an unbiased summary is critically low. Beyond the checklist, the main problem for claims is what the number means: an odds ratio between the top rank of ten different exposure scales and never use, from crude data, extrapolated by a linear model. The review may be cited for the existence and approximate shape of a crude gradient across the studies it pooled, for the study-level estimates and as a pointer to the primary studies; it should not be cited for a causal effect, an adjusted effect size, the risk at a stated frequency or potency, or for the absence of a safe level of use.

key_findings.finding: 571 records from the database search; 442 excluded on title or abstract; 129 full texts plus 4 studies from reference lists assessed; 115 excluded at full text (53 unsuitable outcome, 21 unsuitable cannabis data, 30 case-only or high-risk samples, 11 not primary studies); 18 studies entered the systematic review and 10 the meta-analysis. Three of the four studies found by hand were reports of the Swedish 1969 conscript cohort.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (flow diagram, an image read on screen)

key_findings.finding: The ten pooled studies include 66,816 individuals: six prospective cohorts (USA, New Zealand, Sweden, Germany, England twice), three cross-sectional surveys (Australia twice, Finland) and one London case-control sample (GAP). Editors' sum of Table 1: 4036 people with the outcome and 62,780 without.
key_findings.note: Editors' check of Table 1: every row total equals controls plus cases, every printed crude odds ratio is reproduced from the counts, and the totals sum to 66,816.

key_findings.finding: Pooled random-effects slope b = 1.36 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.68), corresponding to an odds ratio of 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34) for a psychosis-related outcome at the most-exposed rank of each study's cannabis scale compared with never use; heterogeneity I² = 82%. All data are crude.
key_findings.note: The 3.90 refers to the single highest rank (index 1) on a within-study rank scale, from a model that assumes a straight line in log odds; it is not the odds ratio of any reported exposure category.

key_findings.finding: From the same slope, the authors derive odds ratios of 1.97 (1.68 to 2.31) for the median person who had used cannabis (index 0.5) and 3.40 (2.55 to 4.54) for the median person in the top 20% of exposure (index 0.9).
key_findings.note: Editors' check: exp(1.36 × 0.5) = 1.97 and exp(1.36 × 0.9) = 3.40, so these are transformations of the pooled slope, not separate estimates.

key_findings.finding: Study odds ratios at the most-exposed rank: Tien 1990 (USA, cohort) 1.85 (1.33 to 2.57); Zammit 2002 (Sweden, cohort) 6.20 (4.19 to 9.17); Henquet 2005 (Germany, cohort) 5.16 (3.13 to 8.50); Wiles 2006 (England, cohort) 3.04 (1.41 to 6.59); Zammit 2011 (England, cohort) 4.36 (2.38 to 7.99); Arseneault 2002 (New Zealand, cohort) 4.29 (1.45 to 12.70); Degenhardt 2001 (Australia, cross-sectional) 7.45 (3.99 to 13.90); Miettunen 2008 (Finland, cross-sectional) 4.67 (3.66 to 5.96); McGrath 2010 (Australia, cross-sectional) 1.89 (1.32 to 2.69); GAP data 2012 (London, case-control) 4.38 (3.30 to 5.81).
key_findings.locator: Figure 3A (value labels, read on screen); Figure 2 shows the corresponding fitted curves
key_findings.note: Figure 3 is an image; the values are its printed labels. Every study's interval excludes 1.

key_findings.finding: Subgroups: cross-sectional and case-control studies 3.99 (2.50 to 6.37), 4 studies; cohort studies 3.83 (2.34 to 6.29), 6 studies; psychotic symptoms 3.59 (2.42 to 5.32), 8 studies; diagnosis of schizophrenia or psychotic disorder 5.07 (3.62 to 7.09), 2 studies (Swedish conscript admissions 6.20; London first-episode data 4.38).
key_findings.note: The diagnosis subgroup rests on two studies, one of them the authors' own data; the New Zealand schizophreniform-disorder outcome is plotted with the symptom studies (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Meta-regression on study year was not significant (p = .53); Egger's test p = .79 and Begg's test p = .86 for small-study effects.

Editors' calculation from the ten study estimates in Figure 3 (DerSimonian and Laird; it reproduces the pooled 3.90 [2.84 to 5.35] and I² of 82%): Q = 49.3 on 9 degrees of freedom, tau² = 0.19, and a 95% prediction interval for the odds ratio in a new comparable study of about 1.3 to 11.5. Within subgroups, I² is about 80% (cohort), 87% (cross-sectional), 82% (symptoms) and 50% (diagnosis, 2 studies).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: standard errors derived from the printed 95% intervals on the log scale; prediction interval with t on 8 degrees of freedom. The paper reports none of these quantities.

key_findings.finding: The category-level crude odds ratios do not rise steadily in several studies: London case-control data 0.70 (once or twice), 0.40 (a few times a year), 0.65 (a few times a month), 1.24 (more than once a week), 3.51 (every day); Swedish conscripts 0.56 (1 occasion), 0.98 (2 to 4), 1.90 (5 to 10), 3.24 (11 to 50), 6.71 (more than 50), rising steadily across the exposed categories but below the never-use reference at the two lowest; US cohort 0.84 (moderate use), 2.17 (daily use); English cohort of Zammit 2011, 2.07, 3.11, 1.42 (1 case) and 5.69 (3 cases) across rising categories; Finnish adolescents 2.62 after a single use and 3.00 for regular use.

Method: never use is given index 0 and people who had used an index between 0 and 1 by rank, in bins whose widths follow the group counts; 1000 simulation iterations per study; studies weighted by the standard error of the slope and pooled “under the assumption of an equivalent distribution of cannabis use across studies”.
key_findings.note: In the London case-control sample, 473 of 798 participants are cases, and in the Finnish survey 31% are counted as cases, so their bins reflect the sampling or the screening threshold rather than the population's use (editors' observation from Table 1).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the estimates rest on unadjusted data and may be partly explained by confounders such as ethnicity or socioeconomic status, citing two studies that controlled for them (refs 16 and 19) as confirming the association; and that, because cohort studies enrolling people with symptoms at baseline were excluded, reverse causation is unlikely.
key_findings.note: The reverse-causation argument applies at most to the six cohorts; three cross-sectional surveys and one case-control study measured exposure and outcome at the same time or retrospectively.

key_findings.finding: Compared with Moore et al. (2007), whose pooled odds ratios the authors give as 1.4 for any use and 2.1 for severe use, the authors say that applying Moore's average 45% attenuation for full adjustment to their top-20% estimate (3.4) would give comparable results; they also cite an adjusted odds ratio of 3.69 (2.49 to 5.47) for a psychosis diagnosis with lifetime cannabis dependence from a US national survey (Davis et al., 2013).
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures: 1.4 and 2.1 from Moore et al. (2007), 3.69 from Davis et al. (2013). The attenuation calculation is not shown; reducing 3.4 by 45% gives about 1.9 on the odds-ratio scale or about 2.3 on the excess odds (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: The authors report having no data on cannabis potency, the period of use or the time between regular use and illness onset; they pooled different kinds of exposure measure (frequency, duration, diagnoses of use, abuse or dependence) because all were ordered, and outcomes ranging from self-reported psychotic experiences to admission for schizophrenia; their estimates assume a linear increase in risk with level of use.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 cites reference 13 for the German prospective cohort (Henquet et al.), but reference 13 is a 2005 Schizophrenia Bulletin review by Henquet, Murray, Linszen and van Os on the environment and schizophrenia, not a cohort report; the primary cohort paper is not in the reference list.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of one of the ten pooled studies cannot be identified from the paper; claim writers must not cite reference 13 as the German cohort.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 and the Results (2nd paragraph) list schizophreniform disorder at age 26 (New Zealand, Arseneault 2002) among the diagnostic outcomes, but Figure 3B plots this study in the psychotic-symptoms subgroup, leaving two studies in the diagnosis subgroup.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Figure 3B
reporting_issues.consequence: The stronger association for diagnosed disorder (5.07) rests on two studies, one being the authors' own; the classification of the New Zealand study is inconsistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The eligibility criteria name cohort and cross-sectional studies only, but a case-control study (GAP data) is pooled, and Figure 3A places it in the cross-sectional subgroup.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Figure 3A
reporting_issues.consequence: The cross-sectional subgroup mixes surveys and a case-control sample; the design comparison is less informative than presented.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria and abstract require cannabis use measured before the onset of psychosis, but three pooled studies are cross-sectional surveys in which use and symptoms were measured at the same time (Table 1).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: For four of ten studies the temporal order is not established, which undercuts the discussion's argument against reverse causation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results cite two references (17, 36) for the exclusion of continuous-outcome studies, while Figure 1 reports three such exclusions, plus one study without the necessary data; two of the eight unpooled systematic-review studies are therefore not identified.
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection of the pooled set cannot be fully reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods state that heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I², but only I² is reported; Q, tau², study weights and subgroup heterogeneity are absent.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical Analysis, 5th paragraph; Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot judge the spread of true effects; the editors' recomputation (tau² 0.19, prediction interval about 1.3 to 11.5) is needed for any claim about consistency.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 2 speaks of an estimated risk ratio while its axis and all analyses are odds ratios.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; with outcomes as common as 31% in the Finnish screen, odds ratios and risk ratios differ, so the quantities should not be described as risk ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference-list errors: reference 9 is given as 'Adverse health effects of medical cannabis use' (Lancet 2009), while the Hall and Degenhardt Lancet 2009 review held in this project (hall_2009) is titled 'Adverse health effects of non-medical cannabis use'; several entries carry implausible page fields (for example Arseneault 2002, BMJ 325:2; Degenhardt 2001, Psychol Med 31:10; Zammit 2011, Br J Psychiatry 199:6).
reporting_issues.consequence: Match cited studies by DOI rather than by the printed citation.

disagreements.first_pass: Often cited as the dose-response meta-analysis for cannabis and psychosis. Its pooled figure is a crude odds ratio extrapolated to the top rank of ten different exposure scales and should only be cited with that description; it cannot give the risk at a stated frequency or potency. The review discusses no critique of a causal reading and no genetic (Mendelian randomization, polygenic score, co-relative) or quasi-experimental test. The London case-control data inside it overlap Di Forti et al. (2009, 2014 and 2015), and its overlap with Moore et al. (2007) should be checked against sc_moore_2007 before the two are counted as independent.
